title: 25. systemd, Services & Boot
content:
# 25. systemd, Services & Boot

On many Linux distributions, systemd manages services, timers, logs, dependencies, and boot targets. Operators need to inspect units before changing them and verify behavior after every change.

## Learning goals

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- inspect service state and logs;
- understand unit files, drop-ins, dependencies, and enablement;
- distinguish starting a service from enabling it at boot;
- make controlled service changes;
- diagnose common boot and restart failures.

## Service state

```bash
systemctl status api.service
systemctl is-active api.service
systemctl is-enabled api.service
systemctl --failed
```

`active` describes current runtime state. `enabled` describes whether a unit is configured to start automatically. A service can be active but disabled, or enabled but currently failed.

## Logs with journalctl

```bash
journalctl -u api.service --since "30 minutes ago"
journalctl -u api.service -f
journalctl -p warning..alert --since today
```

Use time windows to avoid drowning in old logs. Include `-o short-iso` when exact timestamps matter.

## Unit files and drop-ins

Inspect the effective configuration:

```bash
systemctl cat api.service
systemctl show api.service --property=ExecStart,User,Group,Restart
```

Package-owned unit files often live under `/usr/lib/systemd/system` or `/lib/systemd/system`. Local overrides usually belong in drop-ins under `/etc/systemd/system/name.service.d/`.

After unit edits:

```bash
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart api.service
systemctl status api.service
```

`daemon-reload` tells systemd to re-read unit files. It does not restart services by itself.

## Dependencies and ordering

Units can express requirements and ordering:

```ini
[Unit]
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
```

`After=` controls order, not whether the dependency is required. `Requires=` and `Wants=` express dependency relationships with different strictness.

## Restart behavior

Common service settings:

```ini
[Service]
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s
User=app
WorkingDirectory=/srv/app
EnvironmentFile=/etc/app/env
```

Aggressive restart loops can hide root causes and amplify load. Check logs and `systemctl status` for restart counters.

## Timers

systemd timers are often a better alternative to cron for service-managed periodic work:

```bash
systemctl list-timers
systemctl status backup.timer
```

Timers provide logs, dependency handling, and consistent management through `systemctl`.

## Boot troubleshooting

Useful commands:

```bash
systemd-analyze blame
systemd-analyze critical-chain
journalctl -b -p warning..alert
```

For emergency boot issues, recovery mode and rescue targets may be needed. Treat boot changes as high-risk and keep rollback access available.

## Practice

Create a simple service that runs a local script, logs to stdout, restarts on failure, and reads an environment file. Add a drop-in override, reload systemd, restart the service, inspect logs, then disable and stop it cleanly.
